messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 21
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Media: Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building, Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings
  Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Marcus

Marcus was twenty-one when his younger brother Dominik died. It happened on a Tuesday evening in March, in the parking lot behind the shopping centre where Dominik worked stacking shelves. A dispute over a debt escalated into violence. Marcus was not there. He was at home with his wife, Petra, when the police called. The details emerged slowly—Dominik had been struck repeatedly, had fallen, had struck his head on the concrete edge of a parking barrier. The specific image that would later haunt Marcus was something he never witnessed but could not stop seeing: the back of Dominik's skull, the particular curve of it that Marcus remembered from childhood, now fractured against grey concrete.

In the weeks after the funeral, Marcus found himself unable to be alone. Not because he feared for his safety in any rational sense, but because the moment silence settled around him—when Petra left for her shifts at the hospital, when he sat in the bathroom, when he woke at three in the morning—the smell would come. Not a smell exactly, but a memory of one. Dominik's cologne, the cheap drugstore kind he'd worn since he was sixteen. Mixed with something else. Copper. Concrete dust. The smell was so vivid that Marcus would gag, would stumble into the living room to turn on the television, would text Petra in a panic even though she was working and couldn't answer. Being alone meant being trapped with that sensory ghost, so he stopped being alone. He took to sitting in the corner of the break room at the warehouse where he'd worked, even on his days off, just to be near people. Eventually he stopped going to the warehouse altogether, and then there was no reason to leave the house except to follow Petra from room to room, waiting in doorways while she showered, sitting on the bathroom mat while she used the toilet, his presence becoming a weight she never complained about but couldn't ignore.

When people moved suddenly—when Petra reached for something on a high shelf, when a neighbour appeared around the corner of the street—Marcus's body would jolt as though he himself were under threat. His hands would clench. His breath would come shallow. He was certain, in those moments, that violence was about to unfold, that he was about to witness something terrible again. His body had become an enemy, responding to phantom danger with the certainty of actual peril. He had come to believe that he could not trust his own nervous system, that it was broken, that it would betray him at any moment.

The flashbacks were not dreams. They were vivid photographic moments that would erupt without warning—not memories he recalled so much as scenes he suddenly inhabited. He would be standing in the kitchen and find himself seeing, with absolute clarity, the parking lot at dusk, the sodium lights coming on, the particular angle of the barrier. These moments felt entirely real, present-tense, as though he were there and it were happening now. He could not put any of it into words. When Petra asked what was wrong, what he was feeling, he could only shake his head. The experience existed outside language, a raw sensory fact that had no grammar.

Comments about family—even casual remarks from Petra about her own brother, or a television programme mentioning siblings—would trigger a panic that felt like drowning. He began avoiding all media, turning off the television when unexpected scenes appeared, refusing to read news articles or watch films. But avoidance had its own cost. His unemployment stretched from weeks into months. He had been a competent warehouse supervisor before March, someone who took pride in managing inventory and training newer staff. Now he could not imagine returning to that role, could not imagine being responsible for anything, could not trust himself to function in the world. Petra had begun to mention, gently, that they needed his income. That comment alone—the implication that he was failing her—sent him spiralling into a darkness so complete that one night he found himself in the bathroom with a razor blade, pressing it against his forearm until the physical pain eclipsed the unbearable pressure in his chest. The blood, strangely, was a relief. It was real. It was something he could control.

It was Petra who finally insisted he seek help. She had found the cuts, had cried, had said she couldn't watch him disappear. Marcus came to his first appointment carrying the weight of a man who no longer recognized himself, terrified that no one could help him, but more terrified still of losing his wife to the wreckage of his own survival.
